# 2 Kings Chapter 20 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 241v–242r | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2KI_020_page_481.jpg, 2KI_020_page_482.jpg

---

**1** Around that time, Hezekiah became deathly ill. The prophet Isaiah son of Amoz came to him and said, "This is what the LORD says: Put your affairs in order, because you are going to die. You will not recover."

**2** Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and prayed to the LORD:

**3** "Please, LORD, remember how I have lived my life before you — faithfully, with an undivided heart, always doing what you consider good." Then Hezekiah broke down and wept.

**4** Isaiah had not even left the middle courtyard when the word of the LORD came to him:

**5** "Go back and tell Hezekiah, the leader of my people: This is what the LORD, the God of your ancestor David, says: I have heard your prayer. I have seen your tears. I am going to heal you. On the third day you will go up to the LORD's temple.

**6** I will add fifteen years to your life. I will rescue you and this city from the king of Assyria, and I will defend this city for my own honor and for the sake of my servant David."

**7** Isaiah then said, "Prepare a paste of figs." They made one, applied it to the infected area, and Hezekiah recovered.

**8** Hezekiah had asked Isaiah, "What sign will the LORD give me to confirm that he will heal me and that I will go up to the LORD's temple on the third day?"

**9** Isaiah had replied, "The LORD will give you this sign to prove he will do what he promised: Would you like the shadow on the stairway to move forward ten steps, or back ten steps?"

**10** "It would be easy enough for the shadow to move forward ten steps," Hezekiah said. "Make it go backward ten steps instead."

**11** So Isaiah the prophet cried out to the LORD, and the LORD made the shadow move backward ten steps on the stairway of Ahaz — retreating over the ground it had already covered.

**12** Around that time, Merodach-baladan son of Baladan, the king of Babylon, sent Hezekiah letters and a gift, because he had heard about his illness.

**13** Hezekiah was delighted by the attention. He gave the envoys a complete tour of his treasure house — the silver, the gold, the spices, the fine oils, his entire armory, and everything in his storehouses. There was nothing in his palace or in his whole kingdom that Hezekiah did not show them.

**14** Then the prophet Isaiah came to King Hezekiah and asked, "What did those men want? Where did they come from?" "They came from far away," Hezekiah replied. "From Babylon."

**15** "What did they see in your palace?" Isaiah asked. "Everything," Hezekiah answered. "I showed them everything in my storehouses. There's nothing I held back."

**16** Then Isaiah said to Hezekiah, "Hear the word of the LORD:

**17** The time is coming when everything in your palace — everything your ancestors have stored up to this very day — will be carried off to Babylon. Nothing will be left, says the LORD.

**18** Some of your own descendants — your own flesh and blood — will be taken away. They will serve as eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon."

**19** Hezekiah replied to Isaiah, "The word of the LORD you have spoken is good." Then he added, "At least there will be peace and stability during my lifetime."

**20** The rest of the events of Hezekiah's reign, including his achievements and how he constructed the pool and the tunnel to bring water into the city, are recorded in the court annals of the kings of Judah.

**21** Hezekiah died and was buried with his ancestors. His son Manasseh succeeded him as king.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Verse 1 — The death sentence:** Isaiah's message is as blunt as a prophet can be: "You are going to die." No qualifications, no hope offered. This makes what follows all the more remarkable — a death sentence from God, reversed by prayer. It raises one of the deepest questions in the Bible: can prayer change God's mind? This chapter says yes.

**Verse 3 — Facing the wall:** Hezekiah turns to the wall — away from the room, away from the prophet, away from everything except God. It is a gesture of absolute privacy in prayer. He does not argue theology or claim special status. He simply says: remember how I lived. And he weeps. The weeping is as much prayer as the words.

**Verse 11 — The stairway of Ahaz:** The sign takes place on Ahaz's steps — the structure built by Hezekiah's faithless father. The shadow going backward on those steps is a reversal in every sense: time reversed on apostasy's monument. The good son's miracle is written on the bad father's architecture.

**Verse 13 — "He showed them everything":** This is where Hezekiah's story takes its darkest turn. The man who trusted God against Assyria now proudly displays his wealth to Babylonian diplomats. The narrator repeats it for emphasis: "There was nothing... he did not show them." It is not a sin of rebellion but of vanity. He forgets that everything he has comes from the God who healed him and delivered his city. The Babylonians are not tourists — they are scouts.

**Verse 19 — "At least there will be peace in my lifetime":** This is perhaps the most morally ambiguous verse in Kings. Hezekiah has just been told that his descendants will be castrated and enslaved in Babylon. His response: "That's fine — it won't happen to me." After twenty chapters of building him up as the ideal king, the narrator lets Hezekiah's last recorded words reveal a shocking selfishness. The man who prayed for his city now shrugs at his grandchildren's fate. It is a devastating final portrait — and it explains why his son Manasseh will be Judah's worst king. Something was broken in this house.

*— PNEUMA*
